source.title: Appendix L -- Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, Council, 26 February 2026 (doc 32193)

facts.note: Treasury Portfolio table [App L p.10]. officer.subject: Your PWLB book ties to the pound, and your MRP annuity runs off a rate we publish daily
officer.body:
Dear Kirsty,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more -- the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief -- in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on Appendix L -- the Treasury Management Strategy -- that went to Council on 26 February. You're not being singled out -- every authority gets one of these -- and there's no agenda in it. The paper is unusually clean and the balance sheet ties across all five years, so this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

On the reconciliation: paragraph 5.1.2 prints PWLB external borrowing at 15 December 2025 as £14,349k, and our file at the same date holds seven loans totalling £14,349,128 at a weighted 4.31%. That is £128 of difference across a £14.3m book, or 0.001% -- to the thousand, it ties. That kind of match is rarer than it should be, and we can build every other observation on top of it.

One feature of the MRP policy that caught our eye. Sections 4.2.1(b) and 4.2.1(e) both anchor your annuity method to 'the prevailing PWLB interest rate for a loan with a term equivalent to the estimated life of the project'. Very few councils name a rate that granular in their statement; more typically the annuity rate is set at outset and left there. Your charge moves with a rate we publish daily on both fixings -- so where officers are picking a term for a specific asset, having the certainty rate to hand at the point of the calculation is useful. The 5, 10, 25 and 50-year certainty rates are on the dashboard at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

The distinctive shape of the paper -- and it is quite distinctive -- is the negative liability benchmark. The chart on page 8 sits between roughly (£33m) and (£40m) across the whole horizon shown, and paragraph 3.2.4.1 explains it clearly: 'For Rutland, the benchmark shows the Council is in an asset position rather than a liability position, which is positive as it reflects strong reserves and balances held for future capital investment.' A cash-rich council whose LB measures the cushion rather than the gap is a rare frame in the papers we've read, and the honest way you present it -- alongside paragraph 3.2.4.2 flagging the Leicestershire-allocation constraint on the debt itself -- is a much clearer treatment than most.

One data point rather than a comment. On today's PWLB certainty curve every one of the seven inherited PWLB loans sits below par -- indicative net discount around £2.4m across the book, or roughly 16.7% of principal, because 4.20-4.40% coupons are below current 25-50y certainty rates of 5.30-6.01% (using the rates your section 5.4.2 prints at 22 December 2025). That is INDICATIVE ONLY -- only the DMO can quote a repayment, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment on top -- so please read it as a data point from the same DMO curve you can see any day at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, not as a suggestion. Your paragraph 5.8.4 confirms £2.6m repaid in 2024/25 and £4.5m in 2025/26, and paragraph 5.5.1 frames that as opportunity-driven, so this is very much a running assessment on your side already.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway is becoming central to how the strategy is framed. An interactive version tied to our rate feeds sits at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity -- for a Council whose benchmark stays negative but whose fund balances fall £59.8m to £26.0m across the MTFS, being able to move the reserves path and see when the crossover would occur is the useful thing.

On training, three fit Rutland's shape. MRP policy in practice ties directly to your annuity-method disclosure at 4.2.1. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice speaks to the (unusual) net-creditor framing. And Reading the PWLB certainty curve covers the mechanics behind the discount position on the loan book. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are available for the whole finance team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free -> https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn -> https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

cross_council_observations.mrp_annuity_pwlb_rate: Rutland joins Tower Hamlets and Derbyshire in explicitly anchoring the annuity-method MRP to the prevailing PWLB rate for the matching term. Draft names this as a feature of Rutland's paper without cross-referring to other councils, per PIPELINE convention on comparisons.
cross_council_observations.negative_liability_benchmark: Of the 77 councils read to date, very few present a materially negative liability benchmark. Draft mentions this qualitatively ('rare frame in the papers we've read') without ranking or naming.

officer.voice: Russell Tew, first-person. Not templated: no bold headers, no bulleted summary, contractions throughout. Leads with the exact reconciliation (the strongest single hook), then the MRP annuity anchor (a genuine feature, not a criticism), then the negative-LB shape (Rutland's most distinctive characteristic), then the discount position framed as an indicative data point on the DMO curve (with all four disclaimers: indicative only, DMO only can quote, no MRP/accounting modelled, Rutland is already doing this), then liability-benchmark pathway (standing inclusion), then targeted courses. Deliberately no numerical rate-move claim -- no reliable current PWLB certainty rates to hand at the point of drafting.
